How does the IoC/DI container work? Bean scopes and lifecycle?

The container [[g:inverts control]]: you declare beans, the container creates/wires/manages their lifecycle.

DI removes manual `new` calls → easier to test (mock), easier to swap out.

**Scope:**
- [[b:singleton]] (default): 1 instance/context
- [[b:prototype]]: a new instance every time it's fetched
- web scope: [[b:request/session]]

**Lifecycle:** instantiate → DI → `@PostConstruct` → use → `@PreDestroy`.

:::warn Trap
injecting prototype into a singleton → [[r:it's only created once]]. You need `ObjectProvider`/`@Lookup` to get a fresh instance each time.
:::

:::deep
The container has two phases:
- [[b:BeanDefinition]]: reads metadata (can be modified via `BeanFactoryPostProcessor`)
- [[b:instantiation]]: DI, `BeanPostProcessor` wraps the AOP proxy

Prefer [[g:constructor injection]] (immutable, easy to test, detects circular dependencies at startup) over field injection (hides dependencies, hard to test, forces reflection).

- a circular dependency between two constructor-injected singletons → [[g:fail-fast]] (good); fix by splitting responsibilities, [[r:don't use `@Lazy` to hide a design smell]]
- request/session scope needs a scoped proxy to be injected into a singleton
:::
How does @Transactional actually run? Why does self-invocation lose the transaction?

When transaction management is configured in the default `proxy` mode, Spring uses an [[g:AOP proxy]] (JDK dynamic proxy if there's an interface, CGLIB if it's a class). The proxy opens/commits/rolls back the tx around the method. The logic lives in the outer proxy, [[o:not in the bean's own bytecode]]. [[r:Self-invocation]]: calling `this.method()` within the same bean → goes straight to `this`, bypassing the proxy → the annotation has no effect. - fix: split into a separate bean, self-injection, or AspectJ weaving - similarly: `private`/`final` methods can't be proxied **Code where the transaction is silently lost:** 
@Service
class BookingService {
    
    public void confirmAll(List<Long> ids) {
        for (Long id : ids) {
            confirm(id);      // = this.confirm(id) → doesn't go through the proxy → NO transaction
        }
    }
    
    @Transactional
    public void confirm(Long id) { /* ... */ }
}
    
// Fix: split into another bean, so the call leaves and re-enters through the proxy
@Service
class BookingConfirmer {
    @Transactional
    public void confirm(Long id) { /* ... */ }
}
:::warn Money trap by default only RuntimeException/Error trigger rollback. A checked exception [[r:does NOT auto-rollback]] unless `rollbackFor` is set. ::: :::deep - JDK dynamic proxy (with an interface) vs CGLIB (subclass — can't proxy `final`/`private`/`static`) - advice sits on the outer proxy → every self-invocation bypasses it - correct fixes: split into another bean, `AopContext.currentProxy()` (needs exposeProxy), or AspectJ weaving (also intercepts self-calls) In the default proxy mode, imperative transaction-resource synchronization is bound to the current [[b:thread]] through `TransactionSynchronizationManager` (`ThreadLocal`). A reactive transaction manager carries context in Reactor instead; it is not a ThreadLocal continuation. `@Async` and `parallelStream` start work outside the imperative boundary unless the worker opens its own transaction. A reactive chain must use a supported reactive manager and preserve Reactor context. [[r:Critical fintech trap]]: calling an external API (PSP/GDS) inside a tx → holds the DB connection too long → pool exhaustion + prolonged locking. :::
Propagation REQUIRED / REQUIRES_NEW / NESTED — when to use each?

PropagationBehaviourUse when
REQUIREDjoins the existing tx or creates a new onedefault — shared commit/rollback
REQUIRES_NEWsuspends the outer tx, opens an independent oneaudit log must persist even if the business tx rolls back
NESTEDsavepoint within the current txpartial rollback back to a savepoint
[[o:REQUIRES_NEW typically needs a second physical connection in a JDBC pool]] → watch the pool; other resource managers can have different mechanics. Isolation can also be configured here (fintech usually uses READ COMMITTED/REPEATABLE READ + deliberate row locking). The propagation annotations are intercepted only when the call enters through a Spring proxy in the default `proxy` mode. Imperative managers bind resources to the current thread. Reactive managers carry a transaction in Reactor context and must support the requested propagation. Do not copy this JDBC table to a reactive flow without checking that manager's contract. **Three nested methods and the resulting rollback:** 
@Transactional                                // TX-1 opens here
public void pay(Long bookingId) {
    ledger.debit(bookingId);                   // REQUIRED  → runs within TX-1
    audit.log("PAY_ATTEMPT", bookingId);        // REQUIRES_NEW → TX-2, commits separately
    promo.apply(bookingId);                   // NESTED → savepoint within TX-1
    throw new PaymentFailedException();        // TX-1 rolls back
}
// Result: the debit is rolled back, promo is lost too (its savepoint sits inside TX-1),
// but the audit row STILL remains — that's exactly why REQUIRES_NEW exists.
    
@Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
public void log(String type, Long id) { /* ... */ }
    
@Transactional(propagation = Propagation.NESTED)
public void apply(Long id) { /* an error here only rolls back to the savepoint */ }
:::deep - `REQUIRES_NEW` suspends the outer tx and typically opens a [[r:second physical connection]] in a JDBC pool → it can multiply HikariCP pressure and deadlock when outer workers hold connection A while waiting for connection B. - `NESTED` uses a JDBC savepoint (not every DB/driver supports it well) **OTA deep dive:** - writing *audit/outbox* entries should [[g:share the tx (REQUIRED)]] to stay atomic with the business operation - REQUIRES_NEW only makes sense when the audit event must be saved even if the business operation fails **Resource-allocation bound, not a normal pool-size recommendation:** for `C_outer` concurrent outer JDBC transactions and at most `C_nested` simultaneously-held `REQUIRES_NEW` connections per outer transaction, use `P_needed ≥ C_outer × (1 + C_nested) + reserve` as a conservative demand bound. Measure `C_nested`, cap outer concurrency, and check the result against the database and fleet budget. If it cannot fit, split the workflow, use an outbox, or avoid nested physical transactions. :::
Spring AOP: how does the proxy work, and what are its limitations?

AOP separates [[g:cross-cutting concerns]] (tx, logging, security, retry) from business logic via *advice* wrapped around a *pointcut*. Spring AOP is [[b:proxy-based (runtime)]]: - it only intercepts calls made *through* the proxy to a Spring bean's public methods - it [[r:does not intercept]] self-calls, private methods, or objects created with `new` If you need more power (constructors, fields, self-calls) → use [[b:AspectJ]] (compile-time/load-time weaving). **Why `private` and `final` methods can't be advised:** 
@Service
class PricingService {
    
    @Cacheable("fares")
    public Fare lookup(String route) { /* ... */ }      // works: called from outside through the proxy
    
    @Cacheable("fares")
    private Fare lookupRaw(String route) { /* ... */ }   // silently does nothing
    
    @Cacheable("fares")
    public final Fare lookupFinal(String r) { /* ... */ } // silently does nothing
}
    
// CGLIB generates a subclass at runtime — whatever can't be overridden can't be advised:
// class PricingService$$SpringCGLIB extends PricingService {
//     public Fare lookup(String r) { ...advice...; return super.lookup(r); }  // OK
//     private/final methods can't be reached by the subclass → advice can never be inserted
// }
:::deep - AspectJ inserts bytecode directly → can intercept constructors, field access, self-calls, non-Spring objects, but the build is more complex (weaver/agent) - ordering multiple aspects via `@Order` (important when tx + retry + logging overlap) - performance: the proxy adds one extra call layer (negligible); an overly broad pointcut makes reasoning harder Deep dive: typical cross-cutting concerns besides tx are retry, rate-limit, audit, metrics — [[r:but don't hide business logic inside an aspect]]. :::
How do Spring application events behave around a transaction, and when does an event have to become an outbox row?

`ApplicationEventPublisher` is an in-process call, not a message bus. By default the listener runs [[r:synchronously, on the caller's thread, inside the caller's transaction]] — so a listener that throws rolls the publisher back.
ListenerRunsFailure doesUse for
`@EventListener`at publish, same thread and transactionrolls back the publisherwork that must be part of the same unit
`@TransactionalEventListener(BEFORE_COMMIT)`just before commitaborts the commitlast-moment validation, extra writes
`@TransactionalEventListener` (AFTER_COMMIT, default)after commit succeedsis lost — the commit already happenednotifying the outside world
`AFTER_ROLLBACK` / `AFTER_COMPLETION`after the outcome is knownlogged onlycleanup, metrics
`@Async` listeneron another threadnever reaches the callerslow, optional side work
// publishing inside the transaction, acting after it commits
@Transactional
public void confirm(OrderId id) {
    var order = orders.get(id);
    order.confirm(clock);
    events.publishEvent(new OrderConfirmed(id));      // queued until commit
}
//
@TransactionalEventListener                          // AFTER_COMMIT by default
void on(OrderConfirmed e) { mailer.send(e.id()); }  // crash here and nobody is notified
**The trap in the default:** `AFTER_COMMIT` fixes "published before rollback", but the work is now [[o:outside]] the transaction and outside any retry. A process crash between commit and listener loses it silently. A write performed by that listener also needs a transaction of its own (`REQUIRES_NEW`), or it joins one that is already finishing. :::tip The line where events stop being enough Optional reactions (cache eviction, metrics, or resendable email) can use an event. Required reactions write an outbox intent in the same local transaction. Topic 09 q3 owns Outbox/Saga/idempotency; topic 08 q7 owns broker delivery. This item owns Spring listener timing and the crash window. ::: :::deep - events keep modules decoupled inside one deployable, which is their real value; they are not a substitute for a broker between services (24-domain-driven-design.tactical-modelling-it.q3). - an [[b:@Async listener loses everything thread-bound]]: the transaction, the security context and the MDC. Propagate what it needs explicitly, or the log line for that side effect has no trace id. - ordering between listeners is `@Order`, not luck — but relying on listener order usually means the flow belongs in one explicit service method. - listeners are proxied like anything else, so publishing from a private method or self-invoking a listener behaves the way `@Transactional` does (03-spring-boot-deep-build.ioc-container-transactions.q4). - in tests, a published event with no assertion is invisible. Capture events with a recording listener and assert on them, the same way you would assert on a message (26-testing-strategy.what-a-test-is-for.q1). :::
Spring Cache turns caching into one annotation. Which of its defaults will hurt you in production?

The abstraction hides a cache manager, a key generator and a serialization format — three decisions you now own without having made them.
Provider dimensionLocal cacheShared cacheDecision and test
TopologyCaffeine is per instance; pods hold separate copiesRedis or another shared provider adds a network and availability boundarychoose acceptable divergence and failure mode
TTL and evictionconfigure per cache name; process restart clears itprovider TTL, memory policy and eviction are shared but operationally mutabletest stale windows, expiry and eviction under load
Serializationin-process objects avoid a wire format but still need version-safe codepayload schema, class allowlist and compatibility must be explicittest old and new payloads during rolling deploys
Invalidationwrite on one pod does not evict another automaticallypub/sub, versioned keys or explicit eviction can coordinate copiestest commit, rollback, replay and missed invalidation
Stampede and syncsync=true may coalesce supported local loads onlyannotation-level sync does not automatically lock across nodesload-test one hot key and bound origin concurrency
Tenant and authority keyinclude tenant, user or authorization dimensions when the value depends on themshared topology makes a missing dimension a cross-tenant leakassert key isolation and never treat a hit as authorization
Failure behaviordefine fail-open or fail-closed behavior when local memory is fulldefine timeout, outage, stale-read and circuit policy for the remote cacheinject provider failure and observe the business fallback
// the annotation is a proxy call, so this self-invocation is not cached at all
public Fare quote(String route) { return lookup(route); }   // bypasses the proxy
@Cacheable(value = "fares", key = "#route", sync = true)
public Fare lookup(String route) { … }
//
// eviction inside a transaction that may still roll back
@Transactional
@CacheEvict(value = "fares", key = "#route")                // runs at method exit
public void updateFare(String route, Fare f) { … }        // rollback ⇒ cache already gone
**The consistency problem the annotation cannot solve:** eviction happens in the application while the commit happens in the database, and the two are not atomic. Between them another request repopulates the cache from the old row, and the stale value now outlives the update. :::warn A cached value is a copy with its own lifetime Once a value is in Redis it survives your deploy. Change the shape of the cached object without changing the key and the new code will fail deserializing the old payload, on every instance at once. ::: :::deep - version the cache name or the key when the payload shape changes: `fares:v3:{route}`. It is the cheapest deploy-safety measure in caching. - [[g:evict after commit]], not during: publish the eviction from a transactional event listener so a rollback leaves the cache untouched (03-spring-boot-deep-build.ioc-container-transactions.q5). - a local `Caffeine` cache is per instance, so ten pods hold ten opinions. Either keep the TTL short enough that divergence is acceptable, or use a shared cache and accept the network hop (10-system-design-rate-limit.framework-building-blocks.q3). - [[o:do not cache what you cannot invalidate]] — permissions, balances and prices at checkout are read from the source of truth, however tempting the annotation looks. - the abstraction is worth it for read-through of stable reference data; for anything requiring precise invalidation, explicit cache code is clearer than annotations spread across the call graph. :::
Why does a Spring transaction work in MVC but disappear in a reactive or asynchronous call?

The transaction boundary follows the execution model. In the imperative stack, Spring commonly binds transaction resources and synchronization to the current thread while the proxied method runs.

A call through `@Async` starts on another executor after the caller may have returned, so it does not inherit the same transaction or resource safely. Passing a JDBC connection or EntityManager into that task is a lifecycle bug, not context propagation.

Reactive transactions use a reactive transaction manager and Reactor context rather than assuming a thread-local continuation. The context must travel through the reactive chain; blocking JDBC work on the event loop is still a resource and latency failure.

Proxy rules still matter: self-invocation, private/final methods, or direct construction can bypass advice in the default proxy mode.

**Choose the boundary explicitly:**
- keep one local transaction around the state change
- write an outbox or durable job for work that must survive a crash
- let the worker open its own short transaction

Propagate only an intentional correlation/authorization context under a tested policy; never copy secrets or a live connection.

Test commit, rollback, cancellation, retry after an unknown outcome, scheduler shutdown, executor rejection, and a reactive cancellation path. “It returned a Future” is not proof that the database work is atomic or durable.
How does Spring Boot auto-configuration work under the hood?

Boot scans auto-config classes (declared in `...AutoConfiguration.imports`), applying them conditionally via [[g:@Conditional]]:
- `@ConditionalOnClass` — is the library on the classpath?
- `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` — has the user not already defined one?
- `@ConditionalOnProperty` — enabled by a property?

→ 'HikariCP is on the classpath ⇒ auto-configure a DataSource'; if you declare your own bean, Boot [[g:steps aside]].

:::tip Bottom line
'convention over configuration' = auto-config + starters. Debug with `--debug` to see the conditions report (matched/unmatched).
:::

:::deep
Boot 3.x and later read auto-configuration from `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports`; older Boot lines used `spring.factories` for this mechanism.

The Boot 4/Spring 7 examples below are a separate generation from Boot 3 defaults, so pin the target line before relying on metadata or ordering.

Boot then orders configurations with `@AutoConfigureBefore/After/Order` and evaluates `@Conditional` checks against the classpath, user beans, properties, and web type.

- writing a company-wide [[g:custom starter]] = an auto-config module + `OnMissingBean` (so other teams can override) + `@ConfigurationProperties`
- [[r:Trap]]: wrong auto-config ordering causes wrong bean overrides; too many conditionals slow down startup

**Condition report as a contract:** run `java -jar app.jar --debug` and inspect matched/unmatched conditions in the `ConditionEvaluationReport`.

A protected `/actuator/conditions` endpoint can complement startup logs.

In tests, use `ApplicationContextRunner` to assert the expected auto-config and back-off behavior.
:::
What is a starter dependency and why is it convenient?

A starter (e.g. `spring-boot-starter-web`) is a POM 'bundle' that gathers compatible dependencies for a single purpose (web = Spring MVC + Tomcat + Jackson...).

One line instead of declaring and aligning versions for dozens of libraries. Versions are aligned by Boot's [[g:parent BOM]].

:::warn Interview trap
The follow-up question is almost always 'how does a starter differ from auto-configuration?'.
:::

A starter is just a POM that pulls in dependencies, [[o:it contains no configuration logic]]; the actual auto-configuration lives in `spring-boot-autoconfigure` with `@Conditional` classes (03-spring-boot-deep-build.auto-configuration-build.q1).

Proof: pull in a starter and exclude auto-config, it still runs; conversely you can declare the dependency yourself and auto-config still kicks in.
:::deep
- a starter is a 'meta' POM (little/no code) that bundles compatible dependencies + activates the matching auto-config
- transitive versions are aligned by the `spring-boot-dependencies` BOM → declaring a dependency [[g:needs no version]]
- upgrading Boot means upgrading the whole 'basket' of libraries that have been tested together (reduces jar hell)
- writing your own `company-payments-starter` standardizes config/observability across services (platform engineering)

[[r:Trap]]: overriding a transitive version in the BOM must be done carefully (can break tested compatibility); use `dependency:tree` to check.
:::
Deep-dive POM: dependencyManagement, BOM, scope, transitive dependencies, exclusion — what do you need to know?

- [[b:dependencyManagement / BOM]]: centralizes version declarations (import BOM with scope `import`); child modules inherit them
- [[b:scope]]: `compile` (default), `provided` (supplied by the container), `runtime` (JDBC driver), `test`, `import`
- [[b:transitive dependency]]: a dependency of a dependency; conflicts are resolved by [[o:'nearest wins']]
- [[b:exclusion]]: excludes an unwanted transitive dependency
- distinguish *plugin* (build-time) from *dependency* (the app's libraries)

Golden command: `mvn dependency:tree` to inspect and untangle conflicts.

:::tip Bottom line
transitive + nearest-wins + BOM are the key to avoiding 'jar hell' and `NoSuchMethodError` caused by version mismatches.
:::

:::deep
- [[o:nearest-wins]] resolves conflicts (shallowest depth wins, NOT the highest version) → can sometimes pull in an unexpectedly old version, so pin it explicitly in `dependencyManagement` to [[g:'pin']] it
- `<scope>import</scope>` in dependencyManagement imports a BOM (e.g. Spring Cloud)
- `optional=true` stops a transitive dependency from propagating further; `provided` for things supplied by the container (servlet/lombok)
- `dependency:tree -Dverbose` + `dependency:analyze` (used-but-undeclared / declared-but-unused)

Deep dive: runtime `NoSuchMethodError`/`NoClassDefFoundError` is usually caused by mismatched transitive versions → pinning the BOM + exclusions fixes 'jar hell' at the root.
:::

Spring profiles & externalized config — best practices for managing configuration?

Separate config from code ([[g:12-factor]]): `application-{profile}.yml`, env vars, secret managers.

**Priority order (highest → lowest):**
- command-line args
- env vars
- `application-{profile}.yml`
- `application.yml`
- defaults in code

[[r:Never hardcode secrets]] in the repo; use Vault/Secrets Manager + a config server for multiple services.

:::deep
- do NOT commit secrets to the repo/image; inject them at runtime via env/volume from Vault/AWS Secrets Manager/K8s Secret (+KMS)
- profiles for environment (`dev/staging/prod`) and for features (`@Profile`)
- for multiple services → Spring Cloud Config/Consul + dynamic refresh (`@RefreshScope`) to change config without redeploying

- [[r:Trap]]: a profile-specific override silently causes 'works fine locally, breaks in prod'; storing sensitive config in a ConfigMap instead of a Secret
- config is a kind of API too — version it and audit changes (GitOps)
:::
@Async and @Scheduled — what should you watch out for?

- [[b:@Async]] runs a method on a different thread pool (also proxy-based → self-calls have no effect); configure a dedicated executor, [[r:don't rely on the default unbounded pool]]
- [[b:@Scheduled]] for cron/fixed-rate jobs; with multiple instances you must avoid duplicate runs (ShedLock/distributed lock or leader election)

:::deep
[[r:Production trap]]: `@Async` defaults to `SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor` (spawns a new thread every time, NOT bounded) → under high load this explodes thread count/OOMs.
- you must define a dedicated `ThreadPoolTaskExecutor` (core/max/queueCapacity)
- remember `queueCapacity` must fill up before the pool grows threads toward max (a surprising behaviour)

- `@Async` is also proxy-based → self-calls have no effect, and it loses tx/security/MDC context (needs a TaskDecorator to propagate MDC/trace id)
- `@Scheduled` across N instances runs N times → use ShedLock/distributed lock or leader election

Deep dive: Java 21 — a virtual-thread executor (`newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor`) for `@Async` scales I/O-bound work well without pool tuning.
:::
Spring Boot Actuator & observing an application?

Actuator exposes operational endpoints:
- `/health` (liveness/readiness groups)
- `/metrics` (Micrometer → Prometheus)
- `/info`, `/loggers`...

Integrates with Micrometer + OpenTelemetry to export metrics/traces. [[r:Remember to protect sensitive endpoints]] (auth) + only expose what's needed.

:::deep
- Actuator + Micrometer is a [[g:facade]] that exports metrics to Prometheus/Datadog/OTel (swap the backend without changing code)
- the `/actuator/health` liveness vs readiness groups map directly to K8s probes: readiness includes dependencies (DB, broker), liveness only means 'the process is alive' (avoids a restart loop when the DB is slow)
- custom `HealthIndicator` for business dependencies (GDS/PSP); protect `/env`, `/heapdump` with auth

- wire up Micrometer Tracing + OTel → trace_id flows across services; export custom business metrics (`booking_failed_total`) to alert on SLOs
- [[r:Operational trap]]: high tag cardinality (userId, bookingId) 'blows up' the Prometheus time-series → only tag bounded dimensions (status, endpoint). Use *exemplars* to jump from a metric to its trace.
:::
Validation (Bean Validation) and centralized error handling?

Use `@Valid` + annotations (`@NotNull`, `@Size`, custom constraints) to validate at the [[b:boundary]] (controller/DTO).

Catch errors centrally with `@ControllerAdvice` + `@ExceptionHandler` → return a standard error structure (RFC 7807 problem+json).

Separate [[g:syntactic validation]] (at the boundary) from [[g:business rules]] (in the domain).

:::deep
- [[b:syntactic/format]] at the boundary: DTO + `@Valid` + JSR-380 (`@NotNull`, `@Email`, `@Positive`), validation groups for create vs update
- [[b:business rules]] in the domain: e.g. 'seat count ≤ passenger count' belongs to the aggregate, not an annotation
- custom constraints for reusable rules (valid airport code)
- centralized error handling with `@RestControllerAdvice` → problem+json with field errors

- [[r:Trap]]: validating on the client and then trusting it — you must re-validate on the server (never trust input)
- cross-field validation (return date > departure date) uses a class-level constraint; don't cram complex business rules into an annotation
:::
How do you configure HikariCP in Spring Boot for a high-traffic service?

Treat HikariCP as a [[g:bounded admission-control boundary]], not a knob that makes the database faster. With `spring-boot-starter-jdbc` or `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa`, Spring Boot brings HikariCP onto the classpath and prefers it when auto-configuring a pooled `DataSource`. Configure the pool only after defining a fleet-wide connection budget and a deadline hierarchy. 
spring:
  datasource:
    hikari:
      pool-name: booking-write
      maximum-pool-size: 12       # illustrative; derive from measured capacity + fleet budget
      connection-timeout: 1500    # milliseconds waiting to borrow; not connect/query time
      validation-timeout: 500     # must be < connectionTimeout
      max-lifetime: 1740000       # only if infrastructure max age is known to be 30 min
      keepalive-time: 120000      # only when idle paths otherwise expire connections
The numbers above are a configuration-shape example, [[r:not defaults or a recommendation]]. In particular: - derive `maximumPoolSize` from the database's measured sustainable concurrency and the aggregate budget across peak replicas, rollout surge, jobs, migrations, and every `DataSource`; - if `minimumIdle` is left unset, Hikari defaults it to `maximumPoolSize`, effectively keeping a fixed-size pool; set it lower only when fewer idle sessions are worth slower refill during a burst; - `connectionTimeout` bounds only the wait for a pool slot. JDBC connect, socket/read, statement, transaction, lock, and HTTP-request deadlines are different controls; - `maxLifetime` retires a physical connection after it is returned; keep it below a *known maximum-age* limit. `keepaliveTime` pings only idle connections and must be lower than `maxLifetime`; - `leakDetectionThreshold` reports a connection checked out for too long. It is evidence of a possible leak or long transaction, not proof of either; - prefer JDBC4 `Connection.isValid()`; do not add `connectionTestQuery` unless the driver actually lacks JDBC4 validation. :::warn Transaction boundary Never perform remote HTTP, broker, filesystem, or user-waiting work after a transaction has acquired a connection. A 100 ms SQL operation inside a 5 s transaction occupies a pool slot for roughly 5 s, so the bottleneck is hold time rather than query time. ::: :::deep Watch active, idle, pending, acquisition timeouts, acquisition duration, usage duration, and creation failures through Actuator's `jdbc.connections` and Hikari-specific metrics. A growing pending queue means demand is waiting; it does not tell you whether the cause is a small pool, a saturated database, a lock, a leaked connection, or a slow external call inside the transaction. Generic sizing logic lives in (25-microservice.02-pool-exhaustion-connection-thread.q1), while exact Hikari parameter semantics are in (25-microservice.02-pool-exhaustion-connection-thread.q3). The Spring lifecycle and engine-specific resource effects are covered in (03-spring-boot-deep-build.auto-configuration-build.q12), (03-spring-boot-deep-build.auto-configuration-build.q13), and (03-spring-boot-deep-build.auto-configuration-build.q14). **Fleet budget worksheet:** let `B_db` be the database connection/process budget. Subtract administrative, replication, other-application and failover reserves. Require `Σ(replicas_i × poolMax_i) + nested-connection headroom + jobs ≤ B_db − reserves`. The per-pod pool value is an allocation bound, not a normal-size recommendation. Test maxSurge and the largest `REQUIRES_NEW` demand before choosing it. :::

How does Spring Boot wire HikariCP, and what happens from @Transactional to Connection.close()?

Spring Boot's `DataSourceAutoConfiguration` creates a pooled `DataSource` only when JDBC classes and a usable driver are present and the application has not supplied its own `DataSource`. Boot prefers HikariCP when it is available. Common credentials and URL bind from `spring.datasource.*`; implementation-specific properties bind from `spring.datasource.hikari.*`. Defining a custom `DataSource` makes the relevant auto-configuration back off, so multiple data sources also require explicit pool names, transaction managers, `@Primary` decisions, and metrics tags. The imperative request path is approximately: 
HTTP request
  -> TransactionInterceptor
  -> JpaTransactionManager / DataSourceTransactionManager
  -> HikariDataSource.getConnection()
  -> Hikari proxy Connection
  -> JDBC driver + socket/TLS
  -> database session/backend
    
Connection.close()
  -> close tracked statements / roll back unfinished work / reset dirty state
  -> return the physical connection to Hikari's idle collection
  -> physically close only on eviction, failed validation, retirement, or pool shutdown
`getConnection()` borrows an idle physical connection or creates one while the pool is below `maximumPoolSize`. When every connection is in use, the caller waits up to `connectionTimeout`. The object returned to application code is a proxy: calling `close()` releases it to the pool instead of closing the database socket. Spring's transaction manager or Hibernate binds the borrowed connection to the current imperative transaction, so repository calls inside that boundary share it until commit/rollback and cleanup. This has three important consequences: - [[b:Transaction duration is connection hold time]] once a connection has been acquired. Query speed alone cannot explain pool pressure. - Hikari must reset observable state such as auto-commit, read-only, transaction isolation, catalog/schema, and network timeout before reuse. Application code must still close `ResultSet`/`Statement`/`Connection` deterministically; pool cleanup is a safety net, not an ownership model. - `spring.datasource.connection-fetch=lazy` in the Boot 4.1 generation can wrap the auto-configured pool so a transaction that never creates a JDBC `Statement` never borrows a physical connection. It does not make SQL non-blocking or increase database capacity. **What exists in application memory per physical connection?** Hikari keeps pool bookkeeping and proxy state; the driver owns protocol/session objects, prepared-statement metadata or caches when enabled, authentication/TLS state, and socket buffers/file descriptors. Active `ResultSet`, LOB buffers, ORM entities, Hibernate's first-level cache, and DTO materialization usually dominate request memory, but they are request/transaction state rather than an idle Hikari entry. A larger pool indirectly permits more of that active work to exist concurrently. :::warn Hidden connection retention `@Transactional` around a remote call, a streaming response, an unbounded cursor, or slow application computation can retain a connection long after SQL stops. ::: Open EntityManager in View extends the persistence context and permits late SQL during rendering, which can hide N+1 queries and acquire connections outside the intended service boundary; prefer `spring.jpa.open-in-view=false` plus explicit fetch plans/DTOs. :::deep Leaving `minimumIdle` unset gives Hikari a fixed-size target because its default equals `maximumPoolSize`. That favors burst responsiveness but makes every pod try to maintain its full allotment, which matters during cold starts and rolling deployments. An elastic pool (`minimumIdle` lower than max) reduces idle sessions but can create a connection storm when traffic jumps; measure authentication/TLS/session-setup latency and rate-limit rollout surge. Choose startup behavior deliberately with `initializationFailTimeout`: a service that cannot do useful work without the database may fail fast, while a component designed to start degraded may let the pool retry in the background. On graceful Spring shutdown, the `HikariDataSource` bean closes and physical connections are released; `kill -9`, OOM-kill, or a partition cannot rely on that lifecycle, so database-side idle/session limits and TCP keepalive remain necessary. The proxy and transaction mechanics above connect directly to (03-spring-boot-deep-build.ioc-container-transactions.q2). Pool size and virtual-thread count are independent: cheap waiting threads do not create extra database capacity. :::

It also has no universal MB cost: idle-session baseline, active statement memory, driver caches, TLS/socket buffers, execution processes/threads, parallel workers, and server configuration all vary.

On the JVM side, every physical connection adds at least a Hikari entry, driver object graph, socket/file descriptor, and possibly per-connection prepared-statement metadata/cache. The expensive amplification is often *indirect*: N active connections permit N concurrent result sets, ORM persistence contexts, LOB reads, JSON mappings, and database work areas. Therefore JVM heap, native/kernel socket memory, and database memory must be measured separately under the same concurrency. **Source scope and unresolved target:** these rows are scoped to the named documentation lines, not every release, driver or topology. If the application is not pinned to these targets, treat the DB-specific answer as unresolved and verify the exact server and driver manuals before sizing. - MySQL 8.4 server system variables - PostgreSQL current connection settings and pgJDBC documentation - Oracle Database 26ai PROCESSES :::warn Do not multiply a folklore constant Statements such as "one PostgreSQL connection costs 10 MB" or "Oracle always costs more" erase engine version, extensions, session settings, query shape, shared/dedicated mode and allocator behavior. ::: Measure idle baseline, then the delta for representative active queries and parallelism; use PSS rather than summing process RSS when shared pages matter. :::deep Connection-local caches multiply silently. A prepared-statement cache of K entries on each of N connections can create roughly N×K client entries plus server statements/cursors, while Hibernate's first-level cache is per persistence context and follows transaction/request cardinality instead. Size each cache from hit rate and memory/cursor limits, not because a blog calls it "best practice." Database-side multiplexing changes semantics. PostgreSQL transaction-pooling proxies, Oracle shared server/DRCP, and vendor proxies reduce backend/process churn, but session variables, temporary tables, prepared statements, advisory locks, package state, and failover behavior may no longer have connection affinity. Verify the application's state assumptions before inserting another pooling layer, and choose one client-side pool rather than accidentally wrapping a pool inside another pool. Finally, an idle connection is not free, but an active query usually has a much larger and more variable footprint. `max_connections`/`PROCESSES` answers "can another session log in?"; load testing answers "how many active queries meet the SLO without CPU, I/O, lock or memory collapse?" Those are separate limits. :::
How should you budget connections and align Hikari, JDBC, and database timeouts for autoscaling, rolling deploys, and failover?

Start with two ceilings: the database's [[b:hard session slots]] after administrative, replication, HA, maintenance, and other-application reserves; and its [[b:measured safe active-query concurrency]] for this workload. The lower operational boundary wins. Then calculate the worst live fleet, not today's replica count: 
fleet connection ceiling
  = Σ(max live instances during rollout/failover × every pool maximum)
  + batch workers + schedulers + migration clients
    
example only: (8 replicas + maxSurge 2) × (12 primary + 8 replica) + 4 jobs = 204
The arithmetic exposes risk; it does NOT prove that 204 is safe.
Count read/write pools, tenant-specific pools, sidecars, canaries and old/new versions during a rollout. If the ceiling exceeds the assigned budget, reduce per-pod pools or rollout surge, cap replicas, consolidate tenant pools, or introduce a semantics-compatible server/proxy pool. Raising the database's hard connection setting without CPU, memory, I/O and lock evidence can convert a clean "too many connections" rejection into a slow cluster-wide collapse. **Timeouts are layered contracts, not synonyms:**

Spring transaction timeoutTransaction-manager lifetime/resource deadline; it may propagate to JDBC statementsCan mark/roll back the transaction when enforced; it does not interrupt arbitrary Java or remote calls
HTTP/request deadlineEnd-to-end service budget, including response serializationMust be outside the inner budgets and leave time to return a controlled error
maxLifetime/keepaliveTimeConnection lifecycle/idle liveness, not request executionRetirement or health maintenance; neither cancels a slow query
Allocate inner budgets so pool wait + database work + application work fit inside the transaction/request deadline; reserve time for cleanup and error propagation. **Configure driver properties explicitly and verify their units:** - MySQL Connector/J uses milliseconds for `connectTimeout`/`socketTimeout` - pgJDBC uses seconds for the similarly named properties - Oracle documents `oracle.jdbc.ReadTimeout` in milliseconds and has separate Oracle Net connect/keepalive controls Copying the same numeric map across drivers can therefore change a 2-second intent into 2 milliseconds or leave it effectively unbounded. **Diagnose before increasing the pool:**

active=max, pending/acquire timeouts rise, usage duration rises, DB CPU modestLong transaction, remote I/O inside transaction, lock wait, streaming result, N+1, or leaked checkoutTrace connection usage; inspect thread dumps, transaction spans, lock waits and slow queries;
use leak detection only as supporting evidence

How does HikariCP interact with transaction isolation, and how do you prevent connection state leaking between requests?

HikariCP is a pool, not an isolation layer. A physical connection can serve many requests, so the isolation setting belongs to a transaction or workload contract, not to whichever request borrowed the connection last.

- Set a global default only when every transaction can safely use it. Otherwise use @Transactional(isolation = ...) or JDBC setTransactionIsolation before the first statement, and verify that the transaction manager owns the connection.
- Prefer transaction-scoped database settings where supported, such as PostgreSQL SET LOCAL. Do not leave session-level SET commands, read-only flags, schema changes, or catalog changes for the next borrower.
- Close the logical connection on every path. Hikari returns it to the pool and resets the standard JDBC state it tracks; it cannot reset arbitrary session variables, temporary tables, or application side effects.

Pool sizing and isolation solve different bottlenecks. maximumPoolSize limits simultaneous physical database work; connectionTimeout limits waiting for a slot. A larger pool cannot fix lock contention or a database that is already saturated.

When debugging, correlate Hikari active, pending, and usage-duration metrics with database locks, active queries, and transaction traces. If a request sees the wrong isolation, inspect transaction boundaries and session-state leakage before changing pool size.

A safe test matrix uses two concurrent transactions, the deployed driver and database version, commit and rollback paths, and a connection returned to the pool between cases. Assert both visibility behavior and state reset.

**Session-state leakage test:** borrow a connection, set isolation/read-only/schema and one arbitrary session variable, create any temporary object used by the application, then close it.

Borrow again through the same pool. Assert standard JDBC state and application-owned session state are reset or explicitly cleaned; verify the temporary object and transaction outcome cannot affect the next borrower.

Repeat on success, rollback, exception, cancellation, pool eviction and the exact deployed driver/database versions. Hikari's standard reset is a safety net, not proof that arbitrary SQL/session variables were undone.
How do you make a Spring Boot dependency upgrade reproducible instead of trusting a green build?

A green compile proves only that one resolution and test path succeeded. Pin the Java, Spring Boot, Spring Framework, plugin, build-tool, driver, database, and container versions that the service supports.

Use the official BOM or dependency constraints, commit the lock/resolution policy where the build tool supports it, reject dynamic versions, and inspect the resolved dependency tree for convergence, exclusions, duplicate APIs, and known vulnerabilities.

Make repository and artifact trust explicit: use approved repositories, checksum/signature/provenance verification where available, an SBOM, and one promoted artifact rather than rebuilding every environment.

**Test the upgrade with:**
- startup/condition-report checks
- real database semantics through Testcontainers or an equivalent environment
- public JSON/contract tests and migration/rollback tests
- a canary

A build cache may reduce time, but it must not be treated as a correctness oracle; cache keys and task inputs must be reproducible.

Measure build performance as a workload: cold versus warm daemon, dependency resolution, configuration, compilation, annotation/code generation, tests, packaging, cache hit/miss, CI runner and network.

Gradle configuration cache and task cache require cache-safe build logic, so profile and fix invalidation rather than copying a flag. Record the before/after report, rollout owner, rollback artifact, and dependency/security review.

The upgrade is complete only when runtime behavior and reproducibility—not only compile time—are preserved.
How do you route read-only transactions to a replica in Spring, and why does the obvious `AbstractRoutingDataSource` version keep hitting the primary?

**The idea:** one `DataSource` that picks primary or replica per transaction, keyed on `@Transactional(readOnly = true)`. **The trap:** the routing key is read when the connection is fetched. The transaction manager fetches it in `doBegin`, *before* the read-only flag is published to `TransactionSynchronizationManager` — so every transaction routes to the primary, and nothing fails to tell you. **The fix, built in since Spring Framework 6.1.2:** `LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy` defers the physical fetch to the first statement, and can route read-only transactions itself: 
@Bean @Primary
DataSource dataSource(DataSource primary, DataSource replica) {
    var proxy = new LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy(primary);
    proxy.setReadOnlyDataSource(replica);    // used inside readOnly = true transactions
    return proxy;
}
────
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
List<Order> history(CustomerId id) { … }      // replica
@Transactional
Order place(PlaceOrder cmd) { … }               // primary
**What routing does not give you: read-your-writes.** A user who places an order and lands on "my orders" reads a replica that may not have it yet. Decide that per read, not per bean: route that read to the primary, or wait until the replica has replayed past the write (06-db-scaling.replication-consistency.q2). :::warn Make the replica refuse writes on its own `readOnly = true` is a hint, not a guard. Point the replica pool at a read-only standby or a SELECT-only user, so a mislabelled method fails loudly instead of diverging. ::: :::deep - the older recipe is still everywhere: subclass `AbstractRoutingDataSource`, return a key from `isCurrentTransactionReadOnly()`, and wrap *that* in `LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy`. It works for the same reason; the 6.1.2 property removes the subclass. - per the proxy's Javadoc, `Connection.setReadOnly` is left untouched and auto-commit and isolation are expected to match the primary — so configure the replica's Hikari pool with `readOnly=true` and the same defaults. - an inner `readOnly` method called from a writing transaction joins it and runs on the primary connection already bound — the safe direction. - `REQUIRES_NEW` with `readOnly = true` opens a second connection, from the replica pool; size both pools for that (03-spring-boot-deep-build.auto-configuration-build.q14). - replica lag belongs on a dashboard before it becomes a bug report, and a reporting query that runs for minutes on a replica can delay replay itself (06-db-scaling.replication-consistency.q1). - split reads only when primary read load is measured to be the constraint: by the tier yardstick a replica is `not needed` at T1 and `worth it` at T2–T3 once reporting reads compete with writes. :::
`@Scheduled` with fixedDelay, fixedRate or cron — and when do you need Quartz or a job table instead?

**The three triggers:** - [[b:fixedDelay]]: wait *n* after the previous run *finished*. The gap is guaranteed; the cadence drifts. - [[b:fixedRate]]: start every *n* from the previous *start*. A slow run delays the next one; runs of the same task still never overlap. - [[b:cron]]: wall-clock times in a named zone. A time missed while the app was down, or while the last run overran, is simply skipped. 
@Scheduled(fixedDelay = 30, timeUnit = TimeUnit.SECONDS)   // poll a table
@Scheduled(cron = "0 0 2 * * *", zone = "UTC")            // sec min hour day month weekday
@Scheduled(fixedRateString = "${jobs.heartbeat:PT1M}")     // interval from config
**Two defaults that surprise:** - Spring Boot's scheduler has [[r:one thread]] (`spring.task.scheduling.pool.size=1`): one slow job delays every other job in the application. - nothing is persisted: a restart forgets what ran, and every replica runs every job (25-microservice.08-operational-concerns.q4). **When Quartz earns its place:** jobs and triggers stored in the database (`spring.quartz.job-store-type=jdbc`), a cluster where exactly one node fires each trigger, and an explicit [[g:misfire policy]] for the runs the cluster missed while it was down.
NeedReach for
an in-process tick: poll, refresh, clean up@Scheduled, plus a lease once replicas > 1
schedules created at run time, per tenant or user, that survive restartsQuartz JDBC JobStore, clustered
a backlog of work items with retries and an audit traila job table drained with SKIP LOCKED
cross-system workflows with timers that last daysa workflow engine, not a scheduler
:::warn Quartz clustering trusts the clock Quartz requires node clocks within a second of each other, and a non-clustered instance started on the same tables corrupts the schedule. Both are documented; both happen in staging. ::: :::deep - Quartz decides which node fires a trigger by taking a database row lock. `isClustered=true` and a unique `instanceId` per node (`AUTO`) are the minimum; `clusterCheckinInterval` decides how fast a dead node's jobs are recovered. - misfire is the question `@Scheduled` never asks. A trigger later than `misfireThreshold` (60 s by default) applies its instruction — fire once now, or do nothing until the next time. Choose per job; the "smart policy" default is not a decision. - `@DisallowConcurrentExecution` keeps one job key from running twice at once across the cluster; without it, a run that outlasts its interval overlaps itself. - Boot auto-configures a `SpringBeanJobFactory`, so jobs get dependencies injected; but a job is instantiated per execution, so state belongs in the `JobDataMap` or the database, never in fields. - with `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true`, Boot runs `@Scheduled` on a virtual-thread scheduler, so one slow job no longer blocks the rest — the overlap and duplicate-run questions remain. - Quartz's eleven `QRTZ_` tables ship as DDL per database; let Flyway own them like the rest of the schema (14-devops-k8s-best-practices.ci-cd-2026-best-practices.q7). - cron is zone-sensitive: schedule in UTC or name the zone, and decide what 02:30 means on a DST night (01-java-core-jvm.language-fundamentals.q7). :::
The full bean lifecycle: what are the 8 stages, and where do the intervention hooks sit?

The container doesn't just `new` an object — it runs [[b:8 stages]] for every bean. Knowing the exact order is how you answer 'when does the AOP proxy get created' and 'why has `@PostConstruct` already seen its dependencies'. 1. [[b:Instantiation]] — calls the constructor (constructor injection happens right here) 2. [[b:Populate properties]] — sets fields/setters: `@Autowired`, `@Value` 3. [[b:Aware callbacks]] — `BeanNameAware` → `BeanFactoryAware` → `ApplicationContextAware` 4. [[b:BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitialization]] — runs for *every* bean 5. [[b:Initialization]] — `@PostConstruct` → `afterPropertiesSet()` (InitializingBean) → `init-method` 6. [[b:BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitialization]] — [[g:where the AOP proxy gets wrapped]] 7. [[b:Ready to use]] — the singleton sits in the container, serving requests 8. [[b:Destruction]] — `@PreDestroy` → `destroy()` (DisposableBean) → `destroy-method` :::warn Trap [[r:Prototype]] beans: the container creates them and lets go — it [[r:never calls the destroy callback]]. Resources (files, sockets, executors) in a prototype bean must be closed manually. ::: :::deep - `@PostConstruct` runs in step 5, [[o:before the proxy is wrapped in step 6]] → `this` at that point is the [[r:raw bean]]; calling your own `@Transactional`/`@Async`/`@Cacheable` method from within `@PostConstruct` has no effect - if you need to run after the context is fully ready, use `ApplicationRunner`/`CommandLineRunner` or `@EventListener(ApplicationReadyEvent.class)` - `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` modifies the [[b:BeanDefinition]] (metadata — before instantiation); `BeanPostProcessor` modifies the [[b:instance]] (after instantiation). Confusing the two is a classic mistake - BPPs are initialized very early → [[r:don't inject business beans into a BeanPostProcessor]]: that bean gets created before the infrastructure is ready and [[r:permanently loses its chance to be post-processed]] (no proxy → loses `@Transactional`) - `@PreDestroy` only runs on a graceful context shutdown (SIGTERM + shutdown hook); `kill -9`/an OOM-kill skips it → [[o:don't put critical business logic in a destroy callback]] - destruction order is the reverse of initialization order; to control start/stop order use `@DependsOn` or `SmartLifecycle` (with `getPhase()`) **Where each hook sits among the 8 stages:** 
@Component
class GdsClient implements InitializingBean, DisposableBean {
    
    GdsClient(HttpPool pool) { /* ... */ }         // 1 · constructor injection
    
    @Autowired void setClock(Clock c) { }        // 2 · populate field/setter
    
    @PostConstruct void warmUp() {              // 5 · after *Aware and BPP.before
        this.refreshCache();                     // @Cacheable here has NO EFFECT: proxy not wrapped yet
    }
    
    public void afterPropertiesSet() { }          // 5 · right after @PostConstruct
    
    public void destroy() { }                     // 8 · only runs on a graceful context shutdown
}
    
// The proxy (@Transactional, @Async, @Cacheable) is wrapped in stage 6 — AFTER stage 5.
// If you need to run once everything is truly ready: @EventListener(ApplicationReadyEvent.class).
:::
How does a request flow through DispatcherServlet? Filter vs Interceptor vs ArgumentResolver vs MessageConverter?

`DispatcherServlet` is the [[g:front controller]]: it doesn't handle business logic, only dispatches. - [[b:1 HandlerMapping]] — finds the handler matching `@RequestMapping` (path, method, header, produces/consumes) - [[b:2 HandlerExecutionChain]] — runs `Interceptor.preHandle()` in registration order - [[b:3 HandlerAdapter]] — `InvocableHandlerMethod` invokes the controller method - [[b:3.1 ArgumentResolver]] — deserializes JSON → DTO, `@Valid`, `@RequestParam`, `@PathVariable` - [[b:3.2 → 3.4]] — Controller (`@RestController`) → Service (`@Transactional`) → Repository - [[b:3.5 ReturnValueHandler]] + [[b:3.6 HttpMessageConverter]] — Jackson serializes the object → JSON - [[b:4 postHandle]] — only runs when there is *no* exception - [[b:5 HandlerExceptionResolver]] — maps exceptions → HTTP status (`@ControllerAdvice`) - [[b:6 afterCompletion]] — always runs, even on error → cleans up MDC/ThreadLocal **Filter vs Interceptor:** a Filter belongs to the [[o:Servlet spec]], wrapping *outside* DispatcherServlet — it sees the raw request/response and can short-circuit (Security returns 401, rate limiting returns 429). An Interceptor belongs to [[o:Spring MVC]], sitting *inside* DispatcherServlet, so it knows which `HandlerMethod` is about to run. :::warn Trap An exception thrown [[r:inside a filter]] (e.g. a broken token in the Security filter) [[r:does not go through `@ControllerAdvice`]] — it has already left DispatcherServlet. For a consistent JSON error body you must configure `AuthenticationEntryPoint`/`ErrorController`. ::: :::deep - `@Transactional` commits at step 3.3, but Jackson serializes at [[b:3.6 — after the tx has already closed]] → touching a lazy collection at that point throws `LazyInitializationException`. - Fix with a fetch join/DTO projection, [[r:not with `spring.jpa.open-in-view`]] (defaults to true: keeps the EntityManager open for the whole request → holds the connection longer and masks N+1 queries) - a filter that sets MDC/correlation id [[r:must call `MDC.clear()` in a `finally`]] — worker threads are reused, so without clearing, this request's log lines carry the previous request's traceId - filter order: `@Order`/`FilterRegistrationBean.setOrder`; Spring Security is actually *one* filter (`FilterChainProxy`) containing an internal chain of sub-filters - `produces`/`consumes` participate in handler selection and determine which `HttpMessageConverter` is used; duplicate mappings for the same path fail immediately at startup (`AmbiguousMappingException`) - `ArgumentResolver`/`ReturnValueHandler` are customized via `WebMvcConfigurer` — the standard place to implement `@CurrentUser` or a standardized response envelope :::
The JSON boundary is a contract. Which ObjectMapper decisions become breaking changes, and what leaks if you serialize an entity?

Every field name, date format and number representation your service emits is part of the API. Jackson makes those choices by default if you do not.
DecisionDefault riskWhat to set
Field namingJava camelCase leaks into the contractpick one strategy explicitly and freeze it
Unknown propertiesfails on a field the producer just addedignore inbound, so a new field is not an outage
Datesepoch numbers instead of ISO-8601register the `java.time` module, write ISO strings
Big numbersa `long` id or `BigDecimal` loses precision in JavaScriptserialize ids and money as strings
Nulls`null` and "absent" look the same to the readeromit nulls, or model absence explicitly
Unknown enum valuesa new value breaks old readersread unknown as a fallback constant
// the DTO is the contract; the entity is an implementation detail
record OrderView(String id,                    // string: JS loses precision past 2^53
                   String totalAmount,           // string: money never a JSON float
                   String currency,
                   Instant placedAt) { }         // ISO-8601 via the java.time module
//
@Bean Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer json() {
    return b -> b.failOnUnknownProperties(false)   // inbound: tolerate new fields
                  .serializationInclusion(NON_NULL);
}
**Serializing a JPA entity straight out can create three classes of bugs:** - it exposes fields no caller should ever see - it triggers lazy loading during serialization — an N+1, or an exception once the transaction has closed - it welds the storage schema to the public contract, so renaming a column becomes a client-breaking change :::warn Tolerant inbound, strict outbound Ignore unknown fields you receive so a producer can add one safely; never emit a field you are not prepared to keep. Removing an emitted field is the breaking change nobody notices until a client parses it. ::: :::deep - `null` versus [[o:absent]] matters most for PATCH: `{"note": null}` means clear it, `{}` means leave it alone, and both deserialize to `null` in a plain DTO (17-rest-api-design.modelling-resources-uris.q3). - polymorphic typing is where a JSON contract becomes a security decision — bind a sealed set of subtypes, never let the document name a class (13-security-oauth2.secure-coding-at-the-boundary.q3). - mapping DTOs is not busywork, it is the seam that lets storage and contract evolve independently (12-architecture-patterns.clean-layered-building-it-for-real.q2). - always [[g:UTF-8]], explicitly. `String.getBytes()` without a charset reads a platform default that differs between your laptop and the container. - for large payloads, stream rather than materialise: a 200 MB response built in memory is a GC event and a p99 spike, not a serialization problem (15-network-i-o-models.threading-network-programming.q1). - write a round-trip test per DTO — serialize, deserialize, compare. It catches format drift far earlier than a consumer does (26-testing-strategy.what-a-test-is-for.q4). Entity exposure is configuration- and integration-dependent, so “never safe” is not a substitute for evidence. Prefer an explicit DTO/projection and a serialized-field allowlist. Add regression tests for payload size, lazy-load query count, PII/secret redaction and authorization by principal/tenant. Also test unknown/null/renamed fields and old-client compatibility; fail the test when an entity field appears accidentally. :::
